papers.title: What Actually Matters? A Paired Evaluation of Inference Settings for $π_{0.5}$ on BEHAVIOR-1K
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for general-purpose household robotics. However, inference and data-collection strategies that have been deployed in smaller-scale settings do not necessarily generalize to large-scale, diverse task suites. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic, paired evaluation of previously proposed inference and data-collection strategies across all 100 tasks. Our evaluation uses a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ model based on the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner, which achieves a Q-score of 0.39 on the public test set. These results show that proposed strategies do not transfer uniformly to new environments and tasks. Project page, videos, and detailed analysis: this https URL

papers.title: When More Planning Hurts: Learned Planners for World Models
papers.abstract: On PushT, our fixed action updater (1,505 parameters) solves 8 of 16 scenes reserved from our configuration selection. The comparison planners perform as follows: Selected Adam (7 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 218.440s), adapted iCEM (2 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 49.309s), released LePlanner (16 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 5.652s). The total planning and encoding time for our action updater is 59.079s. Note that our action updater does not satisfy the task-cost criterion we fixed before evaluation. We also conduct another matched experiment where we only replay the first ten commands in each context and then allow the next solve 4, 8 or 12 updates (subsequent solves all get 8 updates). Among all 16 contexts (8 scene clusters), the 3 budgets get 9, 8 and 7 successes, respectively. Interestingly, the extra updates did not rescue any failing task in this experiment. All the changes in success/failure happen in one scene cluster, where we observe that the extra updates decrease the costs of the selected latent world-model trajectories for our updater, while the tasks that used to be successes become failures. The code, weights, evaluators, execution traces and cost accounting accompany the paper.

papers.title: Echo: Scaling Visual Reinforcement Learning with Off-policy Experience
papers.abstract: Scaling visual reinforcement learning (RL) with GPU-accelerated simulation is computationally expensive due to rendering and visual-policy inference costs. Consequently, two-stage teacher--student distillation is commonly used to train visual policies, but introduces an imitation gap. In this preliminary study, we introduce \echomethod{}, \textbf{a single-stage off-policy RL framework that scales experience collection without proportionally increasing visual computation}. Through \textbf{inverse distillation}, a state-based auxiliary policy imitates the evolving visual policy and collects inexpensive, unrendered experience. Echo leverages this experience for off-policy value learning, directly improving the visual policy through a shared privileged critic. We instantiate \echomethod{} with FastTD3 and evaluate it on three visual control tasks and two dexterous manipulation tasks in Genesis. Relative to \sdpgmethod{} under the evaluated configurations, Echo reduces time to reference returns by an average of \textbf{60\% across the three locomotion tasks} and \textbf{56\% across both hand tasks}, while improving peak mean returns by \textbf{62\% and 12\%}, respectively. Both hand tasks also achieve higher mean returns at matched simulator-transition budgets. These initial results suggest that scaling off-policy experience is a promising approach to efficient direct visual RL.

papers.title: TACOS: Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision for Visual Footstep Planning
papers.abstract: Humans navigate their environment based on their vision system, anticipating how the ground will respond before committing to a step. Self-supervised learning could provide legged robots the same ability, but the supervisory signal is typically chosen on intuition, and its effect on what the model learns is rarely examined. We present Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision (TACOS), which proposes a meaningful and consistent footstep instability score, based on the residual of a factor graph in legged state estimation. It projects the continuous score into preceding images to supervise a dense visual predictor. We propose two variants, a hard score that exploits hindsight and a causal soft score available immediately. Both metrics are compared against state-of-the-art alternatives in two independent evaluations that share no data or labels. On 1716 manually annotated contacts, both variants outperform every evaluated alternative at detecting instability and ranking its severity, improving pooled severity ranking by 28 % over the strongest baseline. On three outdoor test runs, our metric also trains the most accurate visual predictor, improving rank correlation by 58 % over the strongest alternative, and by a further 25 % when supplemented with onboard context. In a real-world experiment over a 50 m forest trajectory, the trained predictor handles non-geometric terrain properties such as mud and vegetation, while stepping around geometric obstacles like fallen branches. Code is available for reproducibility at this https URL .

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Wrist-Target Construction and Joint-Angle Limits in Humanoid Arm Retargeting
papers.abstract: Motion retargeting maps a demonstrated human movement onto a robot to compute its joint motion. This study examines how the construction of the desired wrist position affects whether computed arm joint angles reach their permitted limits on a Unitree H1-2. A reconstructed target is formed from demonstrated arm directions and robot segment lengths, so its shoulder-to-wrist distance depends on the demonstrated angle between the segments even when no posture-matching preference is applied. A reach-normalized target retains that direction while rescaling the distance, using the same processed demonstrations and the same joint-angle method. Across a forward-reach sweep the reconstructed target places a joint angle at a bound in 10 of 20 repetitions and the reach-normalized target in none. Across 25 recordings from one participant the corresponding counts are 8 and 6 on the reaching arm and 14 and 5 on the supporting arm, and a second participant repeats the bricklaying and lifting comparison. In hardware replay a joint is commanded to a bound in 12 of 16 direction-matching arm-records and in none of the 16 normalized records, and within the eligible records both tracking error and executed torque at those frames exceed their values elsewhere in the same run. Cross-body reach and arm-to-arm clearance identify limits of radial adjustment. The findings support treating target construction and posture matching as separate retargeting decisions, and evaluating both alongside the wrist positions and clearance that manipulation requires.

papers.title: DexSuite: An All-in-One Framework for Dexterous Manipulation Across Arms, Hands, and Tasks
papers.abstract: Human-level dexterity remains a central open problem in robotics, yet few simulation frameworks cover the full workflow of dexterous manipulation, from setting up a robot to collecting dexterous demonstrations and evaluating policies. We present DexSuite, an all-in-one simulation framework for dexterous manipulation built on the Genesis simulator. DexSuite provides 30 tasks and assembles its 10 arms and 12 end-effectors, from parallel-jaw grippers to dexterous hands, into more than 100 single-arm robots and thousands of bimanual pairs. It also ships a standardized environment API, integrated teleoperation, and simulated tactile sensing. Moreover, we define a benchmark of 16 task-embodiment pairs spanning diverse contact complexities and horizons, and release a dataset of 4,700 successful episodes in simulation from human teleoperation, scripted experts, and learned policies. We release DexSuite as open source and hope others will build on it. Videos and datasets are available at this https URL

papers.title: Fundamental Limits of Sampling-Based Reachability: Geometry and Flow Distortion
papers.abstract: Sampling-based reachability estimates reachable sets from finitely many simulated trajectory endpoints. Existing guarantees often control missed probability mass or approximation error relative to the convex hull of the reachable set, leaving the geometric error relative to the reachable set incompletely characterized. We study this error as a problem of support estimation under flow distortion. Our assumptions combine a uniform lower bound on the local volume density of the initial set, a lower bound on the sampling density, and a one-sided Lipschitz constant $\mu$ for the vector field. These conditions admit initial sets with corners and dynamics that may expand or contract. In the fine-accuracy regime, $\tilde{\mathcal O}\bigl(2^ne^{n\mu T}(R/r)^n/(\rho\kappa)\bigr)$ independent endpoint samples suffice for Hausdorff accuracy $r$ using the endpoint cloud. Here, $n$ is the state dimension, $T$ is the horizon, $R$ is the volume-equivalent radius, and $\rho$ and $\kappa$ quantify sampling density and local volume density. For $n\ge2$ and sufficiently small $\kappa$, a minimax lower bound over all estimators based only on independent endpoints matches these dependencies up to a dimension-dependent factor $2\cdot4^n$ and logarithmic factors, within the stated parameter range and when the state domain accommodates the construction. The exponential burden in dimension, and in the horizon for expanding systems, is therefore intrinsic to this observation model. Planar experiments illustrate the predicted effects of corners and contraction; robot-arm experiments show how empirical accuracy deteriorates with dimension.

papers.title: socx: GPU-Accelerated Chance-Constrained Stochastic Optimal Control using JAX
papers.abstract: In this article, we present socx, a GPU-accelerated solver for lifted convex reformulations of linear stochastic optimal control under chance constraints, implemented in JAX. We demonstrate that by exploiting the sparse and independent structure of the problem, distributed optimization can reduce it to simpler problems: independent linear-quadratic tracking (LQT) problems and Euclidean projections onto sets. These simpler problems can be solved in parallel and then coupled using the constraints. To validate our solver, we run it on a hover-linearized 3D quadrotor and show a speed-up of up to $98\times$ over MOSEK and up to $2224\times$ over SCS. socx also solves horizons up to $N=1120$, whereas MOSEK runs out of memory at $N=320$. We present ablations to isolate the key components that enable the speed-up.

papers.title: HiFOR: Hierarchical Foresight with Action-Guided World Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Model
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. Specifically, Hierarchical Foresight Prediction jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Building upon these predictions, Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to facilitate fine-grained retrieval. Furthermore, Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval adaptively retrieves relevant future information from the structured latent world based on evolving action representations during denoising, providing targeted guidance for action generation. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

papers.title: Is It the Curriculum or Just the Easy Start? Benchmarking Unsupervised Environment Design on Quadrupeds
papers.abstract: Unsupervised environment design (UED) methods such as PLR, ACCEL, SFL and PAIRED are compared mostly on 2D mazes, grid worlds and BipedalWalker, while terrain curricula for legged robots are hand-designed and evaluated against a few baselines. We present a benchmark that runs fourteen UED, domain-randomisation and robotics curricula under one protocol on five 3D quadrupeds in MuJoCo MJX: the closed-chain W01-TEK and the open-chain Unitree Go1 and Go2, Google Barkour vB and Boston Dynamics Spot. Levels are vectors of eight interpretable terrain parameters, and all curricula drive the same PPO student at matched environment-step budgets. The evaluation reports success on random and held-out structured terrains, interquartile means with stratified bootstrap intervals, capability envelopes and a level-by-level domination comparison. We compare methods within each robot and report, per level set, the top group of methods not significantly below the best. No method is in the top group on every robot and level set. Methods with easy or low-difficulty training levels, curated or not, fill the top groups on in-distribution random levels of Go1 and Barkour, and of W01-TEK apart from PAIRED+BiBC. The success-driven terrain curriculum from legged-robot practice is in a top group most often, domain randomisation on uniform levels in none, and PAIRED in none outside Spot, where the fourteen methods lie within 3.8 points on random levels of difficulty 0.25. On three robots the leader on in-distribution random levels is not the leader on held-out terrain. We collect the results into a per-robot guide to choosing a curriculum.

papers.title: Learned Terminal Costs for Short-Horizon Model Predictive Control of Autonomous Trucks in Interactive Highway Traffic
papers.abstract: Autonomous highway driving for heavy-duty trucks is a challenging control problem. The greater mass, dimensions and intricate dynamics increase the requirements for cooperation from surrounding traffic in critical maneuvers, requiring a careful balance between safety constraints and efficient long-horizon decision making. Model Predictive Control (MPC) provides rigorous constraint satisfaction but relies on terminal cost which can limit its effectiveness at short, computationally affordable horizons. Reinforcement Learning (RL) captures long-term driving behavior but offers no constraint guarantees and tends toward overly conservative policies when trained under sparse collision penalties. In this paper, we propose a hybrid MPC and RL framework for highway driving in autonomous trucks, where a finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, uses a pre-trained RL model for terminal cost estimation. We evaluate the framework in a simulation environment with reactive surrounding traffic and compare it against pure MPC with zero terminal cost, rollout with terminal cost estimation using a base policy, and pure RL. Results show that the hybrid approach achieves zero collisions with the lowest cost of any configuration.

papers.title: Coupled Guidance for Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Guidance methods are essential tools for steering the generation process in diffusion models, improving the generalizability of stochastic robotic controllers and enabling high-quality controlled image synthesis. Despite strong parallels between flow-matching and diffusion, integrating guidance into flow-matching models remains quite challenging. Recent work has proposed general guidance frameworks for flow-matching, however, they are direct adaptations of diffusion guidance methods and can prove unstable. In this work, we conduct a theoretical analysis of guidance in flow-matching and show that a naive translation of diffusion-based guidance to flow-matching breaks the coupling distribution used during training, resulting in weaker control over sampling accuracy. Building on this insight, we propose Coupled Guidance, a flow-matching-specific guidance mechanism derived from a geometric perspective that leverages the coupling structure inherent to flow-matching training. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experimentation on a custom robotic collision avoidance task using ManiSkill3, four robotic dexterous manipulation tasks from the Adroit benchmark, and three image generation tasks, namely inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring, using the ImageNet-128 and CelebA-HQ-256 datasets. Our findings show that our framework improves sample quality and guidance stability across all tasks, without imposing any additional overhead.

papers.title: Smartphone Indoor Localization Enhanced by Hierarchical Multi-Sensor Context Recognition
papers.abstract: Smartphone indoor localization requires low-cost, robust positioning across scene transitions and phone-use variations. Pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) enables infrastructure-free deployment but accumulates errors from heading drift, structural transitions, and carrying-mode changes. Existing methods often treat contextual cues as a single event stream or local correction signal, limiting their ability to address distinct localization errors. This paper presents a framework enhanced by hierarchical multi-sensor context recognition. A jointly data- and model-driven recognition model predicts environment, scene, and activity probabilities, which are converted into scene-event and action-context segments. Scene-event segments guide scene-constrained PDR correction through corridor heading constraints, landmark attraction, fixed-lag backtracking, and vertical-transition handling. Action-context segments drive action-aware RoNIN-based position compensation for carrying-mode-dependent drift. Experiments on cross-floor and multi-action trajectories against LiDAR-SLAM references show that the proposed framework outperforms PDR and representative learned inertial odometry baselines, demonstrating that hierarchical semantics provide reliable, localization-specific correction cues.

papers.title: Kairos: Semantics-Aware Orchestration of Planning Engines across Classical, Numeric, Temporal and Hybrid PDDL
papers.abstract: Planning at run time, as in robots that re-plan while they act, needs a planner that reads the PDDL its users write (durative actions, numeric resources, time windows, continuous change), answers quickly, and delivers only validated plans. Specialised planners are strong on individual fragments of PDDL, but they differ in coverage, latency and in what their failures mean. We study whether selecting heterogeneous engines from the semantics of each task can give broad coverage of PDDL, from STRIPS to PDDL+, while remaining competitive with specialised planners and making explicit what each answer guarantees. Kairos profiles each task to decide which of five engines apply (ground heuristic search, compressed and snap-action temporal search, time steps for hybrid dynamics, lifted search) and schedules them under one budget of time and memory. Every candidate plan is checked by a validator independent of the planner's transformations, and "unsolvable" is reported only when a search whose exhaustion is a proof exhausts its space. On 1,756 tasks from nine comparative suites, Kairos solves more tasks at the full limits than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite, with the largest differences on numeric, temporal, PDDL3 and PDDL+ planning, and it also solves the most tasks at 100 ms and 1 s. Resampling over domains, the gain is above zero in six of the nine suites, while on classical planning against LAMA it is within the noise. A further 450 feature-oriented tasks and 26 one-feature probes show that Kairos handles all seventeen features probed, where no other planner evaluated handles more than eight. Ablations identify compressed temporal search and the novelty fallback as major contributors, and a comparison with VAL traces every disagreement to a PDDL+ convention or to a documented VAL defect. Planner and benchmark are open source.

papers.title: Smooth Action Chunking Via Movement-Primitive Representations for Imitation Learning
papers.abstract: Imitation learning has become a widely adopted approach for vision-based robot policies, owing to its conceptual simplicity, scalability, and ability to leverage large-scale datasets. As these policies have grown more capable, action chunking has become their standard interface. At each decision step the policy outputs several future actions at once. Backbones from diffusion policies to large vision-language-action models all share it. Whatever backbone produces the chunk, its temporal structure is learned only implicitly. The commanded trajectory is therefore jerky both within a chunk and between successive chunks. On real hardware this appears as visible vibration and as repeated saturation of the follower's velocity limit. We address this issue by incorporating a movement-primitive-based trajectory representation into action chunking. Specifically, a trajectory segment is represented as a linear combination of smooth basis functions, yielding smooth trajectories by construction while leaving the policy architecture, training objective, and inference procedure unchanged. The same representation also yields a closed-form, inference-time correction for the second source of jerk. We condition the predicted coefficients so that the new chunk passes through a via-point at the previous chunk's last commanded action. This correction needs no retraining and, unlike asynchronous Real-Time Chunking, applies to policies queried in one shot. We instantiate it on a one-shot (ACT) and an iterative (DiT) backbone and evaluate in simulation and on a real bimanual ALOHA platform. The representation lowers within-chunk jerk by an order of magnitude on the one-shot backbone and by 2.4 times on the iterative one, with task success statistically non-inferior. The conditioning then removes 73-84% of the boundary discontinuity, at negligible per-step cost.

papers.title: Limit Theorems and Optimal Policies for Flock Flight through Poisson Forests
papers.abstract: Inspired by birds flying through cluttered environments, Karaman and Frazzoli showed that high-speed flight through an ergodic random forest exhibits an ultimate speed limit: above a critical speed, almost surely no infinite collision-free trajectory exists for a single bird. This paper formulates a corresponding bulk-transport problem for many birds. We construct an explicit directed corridor network in a Poisson disk forest and impose a common temporal headway at its waypoints. The maximum current equals a minimum vertex-cut capacity and is achieved by repeated flight along vertex-disjoint paths. The same schedule maximizes completed traversals at every finite horizon, with constant forward speed and no internal waiting. For a forest belt of fixed depth, exact transverse superadditivity yields an almost-sure deterministic current-density limit. A uniform shape theorem for an asymmetric planar dual identifies the current when depth and width grow together. For diverging depth bounded by a constant times width, this current equals the width-first, depth-second limit and is independent of the positive aspect ratio. When diagonal corridors are available, bulk current is positive at sufficiently low obstacle intensity and zero at sufficiently high intensity. For stochastic demand, an upstream admission queue is stable at every rate below the finite-network capacity.

papers.title: PriorMaskMap: Robust Online Vectorized Map Construction with Biased Priors
papers.abstract: Online vectorized map construction provides autonomous vehicles with essential, real-time semantic and geometric scene understanding. While leveraging prior maps presents an opportunity to improve accuracy, they are often biased due to outdated information or temporary road changes. Existing methods, which typically treat priors as fully reliable or only consider limited noise patterns, suffer severe performance degradation when these priors are imperfect. To address this, we propose PriorMaskMap, a robust framework for prior-guided vectorized map construction. Its first innovation is a Prior-Aware Confidence Estimator (PACE) that evaluates the input rasterized map against current visual observations. It assigns confidence scores to regions classified as reliable, erroneous, or blank, creating a foundational mask that guides two subsequent branches. In one branch, the Dual-Prior Query Generator (DPQG) selectively filters and embeds both rasterized and vectorized priors to initialize informative queries from trustworthy map structures. In the other, the Confidence-Guided Prior Fusion (CGPF) module spatially propagates and refines the mask, using the refined version to govern the fusion of BEV features with the prior map, thereby providing rich contextual representations for the map decoder. Evaluation on the nuScenes dataset shows that PriorMaskMap achieves superior mapping precision over existing approaches and exhibits marked robustness when provided with priors containing apparent errors. Our code is released at this https URL .

papers.title: WorldFlow: Joint Video and 3D Motion Prediction via Large-Scale Pretraining
papers.abstract: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: this https URL .

papers.title: Seeing and Imagining as One: Unified Video Generation and 4D Perception for Embodied World Modeling
papers.abstract: Embodied world models should not only imagine plausible futures, but also perceive the geometric, semantic, and motion structure of the evolving world. We present GenSight, a unified embodied world model that brings future video generation and dense perception into a single pretrained video diffusion transformer. GenSight uses a unified spatiotemporal representation for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow. Built on a shared DiT backbone, GenSight uses lightweight task modulation to predict all modalities within the same architecture. All tasks are jointly optimized within a unified velocity prediction space. At inference, GenSight supports two complementary modes: multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step dense perception from an observed video. By unifying modality representation, model architecture, and prediction space, GenSight avoids separate modality-specific pipelines and couples appearance, geometry, semantics, and motion in a shared representation. It promotes cross-modal consistency and allows dense perception to benefit from the spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation. Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception, highlighting the effectiveness of unifying seeing and imagining for embodied world modeling.

papers.title: The Reality Gap in Automated Driving Systems Testing: Landscape, Challenges, and Research Directions
papers.abstract: Simulation is essential for testing automated driving systems (ADS), but discrepancies between simulation and reality can undermine testing conclusions. It remains unclear which discrepancies the literature addresses and what evidence supports correspondence claims. We present a systematic mapping of 235 primary studies that measure or mitigate the reality gap in ADS testing, selected from 4,195 publications. We characterise objectives, targets, approaches, experimental setups, and evaluation evidence. Our classification distinguishes simulated and real-world execution across six ADS test components, separately for each approach and its evaluation reference. This distinguishes real-world information used to construct an approach from evidence used to evaluate its claims. Of the included studies, 76% address mitigation, primarily targeting scenario and actor realism and perception, while 94% report validation or measurement procedures. Only 61 studies report metrics from multiple families covering sensor/perception correspondence, ADS behaviour, vehicle dynamics, or safety outcomes; this coverage does not establish causal links between discrepancies and test verdicts. The synthesis highlights that real-world content and physical execution must be interpreted against the claim evaluated. The findings motivate claim-specific evaluation and component-level reporting to establish which discrepancies affect testing conclusions and when simulation evidence supports conclusions about real-world ADS behaviour.

papers.title: TRIM: Temporal Run-Time Monitoring of 3D Object Detection via Activation Statistics
papers.abstract: Reliable perception is essential to intelligent transportation systems, yet deep neural networks can silently miss safety-critical objects while continuing to produce apparently plausible outputs. Existing run-time monitors for 3D object detection generally assess each frame independently and therefore cannot exploit the temporal evolution of occlusion, point sparsity, and scene complexity. We present TRIM, a lightweight temporal monitor that detects missed-object failures without modifying or retraining the underlying detector. TRIM summarises intermediate activations using compact channel-wise statistics and processes short sequences of these summaries with a temporal convolutional network. Experiments on NuScenes show that temporal monitoring improves AUROC from 0.686 to 0.704 and reduces the false alarm rate at 95% recall from 0.818 to 0.759 compared with single-frame monitoring. Early and intermediate backbone features provide the strongest monitoring signal, while the temporal inference head requires only 0.159 ms on a CPU.

papers.title: Influence of Agent Number and Behavior on Users' Psychological Responses in VR Evacuation Training
papers.abstract: This study aims to build effective drill software by combining a virtual simulation of a disaster with multiple agents capable of expressing emotions. We evaluated how the number of agents and their emotional and behavioral actions during evacuation influence users in a virtual space. The results showed that users tended to act more confidently when many agents evacuated with them, and that the evacuation route chosen by the agents influenced the users' decision-making. These findings indicate that users' evacuation behavior is shaped not only by the environment itself but also by the collective behavior of surrounding agents, underscoring the need to consider how agent behavior affects users' psychological states during training.

papers.title: Forward-Backward Map Matching for Airborne Magnetic Anomaly Navigation
papers.abstract: Airborne magnetic anomaly navigation provides a passive, unjammable alternative to Global Navigation Satellite Systems positioning by matching magnetometer measurements against a lithospheric magnetic anomaly map. Existing map-matching algorithms either assume a Gaussian posterior (extended Kalman filter), require Monte Carlo sampling (particle filter), or discard posterior uncertainty in favour of a single optimal path (Viterbi algorithm). Here we formulate map matching as inference on a chain-structured factor graph and solve it segment by segment using the forward-backward algorithm, which yields a discrete posterior over candidate positions and its Shannon entropy $H_t$ at time $t$. Over the \texttt{Renfrew\_395} map, $10^3$ synthetic trials yield a median position error of $32.7$ m, $91\%$ below the median inertial drift of $362$ m. On these trials and $10^3$ flight paths, the median error is $43\%$ below the extended Kalman filter and particle filter. Across these paths, a threshold on segment-level entropy detects $47\%$ of segments with errors above two map cells and $94\%$ of those above three, at a $10\%$ false-alarm rate. The foregoing results indicate that $H_t$ provides a truth-free diagnostic of map-conditioned navigation ambiguity.

papers.title: Learning from Relative Action Credit for Escaping Local Minima
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning holds the promise of robots that learn manipulation skills from interaction alone, without pretrained priors or demonstration data. In practice, on-policy methods such as PPO routinely stall on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks: dense reward shaping carries the policy through stages, yet stitching them together and discovering sparsely rewarded events rarely succeeds. We trace this failure to the missing action discrimination in state-value credit assignment: a state-value critic judges progress only by episode outcomes, so when the policy converges to a partial solution all outcomes coincide, and improvement stops because no action can prove better than another. We therefore extend PPO with an action conditioned value critic which, can compare the executed action with alternatives sampled at the same state and aid the learning signal. Combined with Generalized Advantage Estimation and a bound on exploration noise, we show how the extended algorithm escapes the plateau and completes precise peg insertion within a training budget where PPO with identical exploration fails.

papers.title: GOFish: Full Field-of-View Gaussian Splatting and Mesh Extraction
papers.abstract: Robots, autonomous vehicles, and consumer 360° cameras use fisheye lenses for wide fields of view (FoVs). Simulation-ready digital twins require photorealistic rendering across the full FoV and an aligned collision mesh. However, prior fisheye Gaussian Splatting methods only rasterize up to 180° and do not produce meshes, while Gaussian surface reconstruction methods assume pinhole training images. We present GOFish, the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method to train directly on fisheye images, rasterize FoVs beyond 180°, and extract an aligned mesh from the same scene. Calibrated densification recovers the surface across the entire FoV, while Calibrated Mip Filtering and Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling keep pixel blur and lens falloff out of the scene and mesh. Across the 200° FIORD and 205° FullCircle benchmarks, GOFish improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 and 1.97 dB, respectively. It also outperforms fisheye rendering baselines within their own FoVs and achieves the highest mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set. Together, the Gaussian scene and mesh form a LiDAR-free, simulation-ready digital twin that renders in real time, ray traces the full FoV, and provides collision geometry.

papers.title: Where Planning Changes the Outcome of Orbital Games
papers.abstract: This paper introduces OrbitalGym, a simulation environment for studying when planning algorithms or system design determine the outcome of adversarial orbital encounters. In an orbital game, two non-cooperative teams of satellites maneuver during rendezvous and proximity operations to win a differential-reward objective. Advances in terrestrial game playing have prompted many methods for orbital games, but studies typically evaluate one method in one scenario, often against a passive or random defender. It is unclear whether better planning matters once vehicle capability (maneuverability, sensing, communications) and adversarial responses are considered. OrbitalGym is a JAX-based environment supporting varying numbers of agents, state representations (position, velocity, attitude, fuel), explicit or implicit communication, and proximity or conical field-of-view sensors. It compiles games to batched GPU code, enabling large-scale parallel simulation of policies across many configurations. This identifies regimes where policy choice affects outcomes and regimes where system capability dominates. We study two close-range games: pursuit-evasion, where one spacecraft tries to capture another, and lady-bandit-guard, where a guard prevents an attacker from reaching a protected asset. We compare PD, LQR, model predictive path integral control, and Monte Carlo tree search over ratios of thrust and propellant, initial separation, game duration, sensor capability, and the definition of capture. In pursuit-evasion the propellant ratio decides most encounters: against five of six evader policies, pursuer policy changes capture probability by 10 percent or more in at most 15 of 90 capability configurations. In lady-bandit-guard, policy matters more: against bandits able to reach the asset, a better guard policy raises defense probability by at least 10 percent in 56 to 74 of 90 configurations.

executive_summary: Several works advance whole-body and navigation capabilities for legged and wheeled platforms: a hierarchical off-road framework uses a low-level RL value function as an implicit cost map within an MPPI planner to achieve safer, more effective goal-directed driving in simulation without explicit cost maps; FORGE learns a reduced-order reference generator plus a whole-body tracking policy to realize agile humanoid locomotion on a Unitree G1 over −2.0–2.8 m/s longitudinal speeds, lateral motion, turning, hopping, and smooth command transitions; Metatron couples a promptable generative base policy with programmable skill prompts so a fixed checkpoint on G1 can execute walking, recovery, teleoperated pickup, sitting, and simulated climbing/acrobatics purely via code-level skills; TACOS defines terrain-stability scores from legged state-estimation residuals to self-supervise visual foothold prediction, improving instability severity ranking over baselines by 28% and terrain-stability rank correlation by 58% in outdoor tests; and a Multi-Layer Navigation System for smart wheelchairs combines virtual-sensor potential fields, MPC, open-vocabulary perception, and priority-based target selection to robustly execute users’ high-level intents—even with faulty inputs—in real-world trials with 10 participants.

New hardware, datasets, and interfaces target richer, safer manipulation: Catch It All! trains sim-to-real humanoid catching policies from a single egocentric camera, using grasp-focused rewards and safety curricula to operate near torque limits and zero-shot catch 9 unseen objects of diverse geometry and deformability on a Unitree G1; DynamicVLA models trained on 1,616 underwater episodes achieve up to 93.3% success (including partials) across three underwater manipulation tasks, while a single-task ACT policy attains 47.9% pooled success (up to 66.7% on one task) in real marine sites, outperforming a SmolVLA baseline; EgoContact provides 22.5K labeled egocentric interaction events to benchmark future contact prediction and, when used as a memory bank, boosts grasp success from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and 16% to 58% on hardware; UMI-Live offers an open-source, self-contained bimanual teleoperation and data-capture system whose datasets enable fine-tuned π₀.₅ and MolmoAct2 policies to achieve 10/10 and 8/10 success on bimanual pick-and-place; and SwapBot introduces modular, tactilely instrumented tool adapters and fast tool-swapping that reduce teleoperation time and workload and yield imitation policies where tactile-augmented demonstrations improve contact-rich tool skills by 15–25 percentage points over RGB-only training.

Multiple works focus on safety, force estimation, and precision in constrained manipulation: an optimization-based active-constraint framework for handheld micromanipulators explicitly models limited workspaces and relative actuation, reducing safety violations by over two orders of magnitude and recovering a threefold accuracy loss seen when enforcing safety alone; FEEL combines a virtual-spring model with an MDN residual to estimate per-finger forces from proprioception with 0–20 N contacts, cutting RMSE by 92.8% versus the spring baseline and by 9.4% versus an end-to-end MDN, and improving damage-free reliability from 7/10 to 10/10 in box pick-and-place; and a straight-skeleton-based auto-labeling pipeline plus SkelGG-CNN produce scalable, geometry-aware grasp labels and predictions, reaching >95% grasp accuracy on Jacquard/Cornell, AP 18.33 on GraspNet novel split, and >95% real-robot success on single and cluttered household-object grasps, outperforming state of the art without domain adaptation.

Several papers propose new learning and transfer mechanisms for control policies: a meta-learned graph neural network leverages semantic, geometric, and relational object histories to rapidly adapt and predict when and how objects move, transferring from simulation to real robots without fine-tuning, outperforming a vision-language model and a class-frequency baseline and enabling near-fastest collision-free navigation in closed-loop simulation; Self-Labeled Preference Transfer jointly trains a shared backbone for preference-conditioned prediction and recognition, then self-labels target demonstrations to reach 96.4% simulation preference-recognition accuracy, 84.8% preference following, and large real-world gains (e.g., 52.5%→92.5% preference following) without extra annotations; a cross-controller transfer framework encodes controller–motion interactions via a transformer context, improving average success by 33 points over naive data pooling and achieving ~50% success on unseen controllers/gains while adapting high-level strategies on contact-rich tasks; Data Inoculation perturbs human teleoperation with an online-trained residual to gather error-and-recovery rich data, yielding policies that match or improve success over standard behavioral-cloning and offline-RL data collection on three real tasks; and ELEVATE lets coding agents reformulate RL problems to learn missing whole-body controllers for a quadrupedal manipulator, achieving 98.4–100% simulated success on tasks beyond the initial controller’s workspace and transferring to hardware with 18/20 and 16/20 successes on rack retrieval and floor-to-rack placement without real-robot training.

institution_matches.title: Open-World Object Motion Anticipation via Meta-Learned Semantic Adaptation
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes a meta-learned graph neural network that uses semantic, geometric, and relational object histories to adapt online and predict, from a few observations, when objects (including previously unseen ones) will begin to move and how objects may move one another. Trained only in simulation, the method transfers to real robot hardware without fine-tuning, accurately anticipating motion of unseen objects and outperforming both a vision-language model and a class-frequency baseline in simulation and hardware experiments. In closed-loop navigation simulation, the method’s motion predictions enable collision-free traversals while keeping traversal time within four seconds of the fastest but collision-prone planner.

institution_matches.title: Catch It All!: Generalizable Dynamic Catching with a Dexterous Hand
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces Catch It All!, a sim-to-real framework that learns policies for humanoid robots to perform underhand and overhand dynamic catching of arbitrary objects using a single egocentric camera, generalizing to unseen objects with varying geometry, deformability, elasticity, and physical properties via grasp-focused reward design and safety-aware curricula. Safety-aware training curricula enable high-frequency action execution near hardware limits, including operation under wrist torque limits as low as 5 Nm. Deployed zero-shot on a Unitree G1 humanoid, Catch It All! successfully performs underhand and overhand catches on 9 unseen objects, including low-rebound plushes, semi-deformable toys, chip bags, and rigid-elastic objects with high rebound on contact.

institution_matches.title: Where Planning Changes the Outcome of Orbital Games
institution_matches.overview: The paper presents OrbitalGym, a JAX-based simulation environment that supports multi-agent orbital games with configurable sensing, communication, and dynamics, enabling large-scale parallel evaluation of planning algorithms and system designs in adversarial rendezvous and proximity operations. In pursuit-evasion games, experiments show that propellant ratio between attacker and evader largely determines encounter outcomes: for five of six evader policies, changing the pursuer policy alters capture probability by at least 10% in at most 15 out of 90 capability configurations. In lady-bandit-guard games, where a guard defends an asset, planning policy choice matters more: for bandits capable of reaching the asset, a better guard policy raises defense probability by at least 10% in 56 to 74 of 90 configurations, depending on the comparison.

institution_matches.title: Value Function-Guided MPPI for Hierarchical Planning and Control in Off-Road Autonomous Navigation
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes a hierarchical off-road navigation framework where a high-level Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) planner uses a pretrained low-level reinforcement learning controller’s value function as an implicit cost map, enabling bidirectional information flow between planning and control instead of relying on explicit cost maps. An online policy evaluation process is introduced to adapt the low-level value function to distribution shifts between training and evaluation, allowing the value estimates to remain useful in unseen off-road environments. In a high-fidelity off-road driving simulator, the proposed value-guided MPPI hierarchy achieves safer and more effective navigation to goal locations compared to a baseline MPPI controller, while removing the need for explicit cost maps.

institution_matches.title: Embodied at Sea: Imitation Learning for Multi-Task Underwater Manipulation
institution_matches.overview: The paper collects 1616 episodes of underwater manipulation in calm and turbulent waters and uses them to train 14 DynamicVLA vision-language-action models with varying proprioceptive configurations for multi-task underwater manipulation via behavior cloning. Across three tasks and 1260 gradable on-hardware pool rollouts, 10 of the DynamicVLA models outperform a baseline, with the best model achieving a 93.3% overall success rate including partial successes. In a marine field case study on grasping and mooring with an ROV at real archaeological and conservation sites, a single-task Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) policy achieves a pooled success rate of 47.9%, substantially outperforming a generalist SmolVLA policy at 7.9%, and reaches 66.7% success on the most successful site-specific task; the paper also releases the BLUEMBODIED KIT for data collection and deployment.

institution_matches.title: EgoContact: Evaluating Physical Intelligence with Egocentric Video
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces EgoContact, a large-scale egocentric dataset of 22.5K manually verified interaction events with pre-contact observations, semantic intents, and pixel-precise contact locations, designed to evaluate future contact-point prediction as a measure of physical intelligence in manipulation. Using EgoContact to benchmark existing methods reveals that current approaches often fail to accurately predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes cannot reliably localize the target object in diverse in-the-wild scenes, even when multiple predictions are allowed. Augmenting an existing affordance-transfer policy with EgoContact as a memory bank improves grasp success rates from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and from 16% to 58% on a real robot, demonstrating the dataset’s practical utility for manipulation.

institution_matches.title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
institution_matches.overview: The paper presents UMI-Live, an open-source full-stack bimanual Universal Manipulation Interface system that integrates cameras, LiDAR–inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power into custom handheld hardware, eliminating the need for external tracking or environment-specific calibration in in-the-wild data collection. UMI-Live includes a simple recording interface and an asynchronous pipeline that performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets, along with software for dual-YAM teleoperation and vision-language-action policy training and inference. Data collected with UMI-Live is validated by fine-tuning π₀.₅ and MolmoAct2 on bimanual pick-and-place, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10 respectively on that task, and the system is further supported by the release of 40 hours of data across three tasks plus complete hardware and software resources.

institution_matches.title: SwapBot: Tool-Centric Robot Manipulation via Interchangeable End-Effectors and Tactile Sensing
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces SwapBot, a modular tool-centric end-effector system that uses low-cost adapters with a fixed robot-side coupling interface to convert common household tools, including articulated ones, into interchangeable robot end-effectors with integrated compact tactile sensing and fast autonomous swapping. User studies in teleoperation show that SwapBot’s design and interface reduce task completion time and operator workload compared to alternative setups for tool-based manipulation. Using demonstrations collected via SwapBot, imitation learning policies successfully execute tool-centric tasks such as cooking tofu, stirring salad, and flipping meat, and ablations indicate that tactile-augmented demonstrations improve success rates on contact-rich skills by 15 to 25 percentage points over RGB-only policies.

institution_matches.title: GOFish: Full Field-of-View Gaussian Splatting and Mesh Extraction
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes GOFish, the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method that trains directly on fisheye images, supports rasterization beyond 180° field of view, and extracts an aligned collision mesh from the same Gaussian representation. On the 200° FIORD and 205° FullCircle benchmarks, GOFish improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 dB and 1.97 dB respectively, outperforms fisheye rendering baselines within their FoVs, and achieves the highest mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set, yielding a LiDAR-free, real-time, full-FoV digital twin with collision geometry.

institution_matches.title: Active Constraints for Simultaneous Guidance and Safety in Handheld Micromanipulation
institution_matches.overview: The paper presents an optimization-based active constraint framework for handheld micromanipulation that can simultaneously provide task guidance and enforce safety, explicitly accounting for the limited workspace and relative actuation of handheld robots with respect to the operator’s hand. Implemented on a handheld robotic micromanipulator and evaluated on a medically relevant artificial task, the proposed active constraints reduce safety violation rates by more than two orders of magnitude compared to baselines. The framework recovers the threefold loss in manipulation accuracy observed when enforcing safety alone, thereby enabling both high safety and high accuracy in handheld micromanipulation tasks.

institution_matches.title: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer for Steerable Robot Manipulation
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT), which jointly trains a shared vision-language backbone for preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition on annotated source demonstrations, then freezes the recognizer to self-label unlabeled target-task demonstrations for policy fine-tuning. In simulation across five types of execution preferences, SPT’s preference recognizer achieves 96.4% accuracy, and SPT attains 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, compared with 59.4% preference following and 88.0% task success for naive fine-tuning without self-labeling. In real-world task transfers, SPT improves preference following from 52.5% to 92.5% relative to naive fine-tuning, and when extended to multiple preferences it achieves 93.8% preference following versus 42.5% for baselines, while maintaining task success without additional manual preference annotations.

institution_matches.title: Robotic Data Inoculation
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces Data Inoculation (DI), a shared-control data-collection framework where a human provides closed-loop teleoperation commands while a residual policy, trained online with the same reward objective as the final learner, perturbs these commands to steer experience toward likely future policy errors. DI’s residual perturbations expose the robot to a wider range of states while the human operator continuously corrects deviations, yielding demonstration data that includes both errors and recoveries and is intended to “inoculate” the dataset against the downstream learner’s typical failure modes. On three challenging real-world robotic tasks, policies trained on data collected with DI consistently match or improve the success rates of policies trained with standard behavioral cloning and offline RL data-collection strategies, indicating DI is an effective way to improve downstream policy performance.

institution_matches.title: Cross-Controller Transfer via In-Context Behavior Adaptation
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes a framework for cross-controller transfer in generalist robot policies that encodes behavioral interaction under each controller via examples of commanded actions and resulting motions, and uses a transformer context encoder to summarize this interaction so a single policy can adapt its behavior in context to different controllers, gains, and compliance settings. Across real-world experiments spanning six controller types and variations in gains and compliance, the proposed in-context behavior adaptation improves average task success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling, achieves 50% success on unseen controller modes and 52% on unseen controller gains, and supports transfer to tasks with limited controller-specific data. On contact-rich tasks such as USB insertion and surface wiping, providing behavioral interaction context enables the policy not only to adjust its action magnitudes to the controller but also to adapt its high-level strategy, supporting transfer across diverse action interpretations.

institution_matches.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents automatically create and iteratively audit realistic robotics simulations and tasks, using an adversarial creation–audit loop and selection criteria derived from U.S. GDP data to target economically relevant physical work. Using this pipeline, the authors construct RoboWorld, a benchmark of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty, on which current frontier models achieve very low performance (average reward 0.06) across all test tasks, indicating substantial headroom for improvement. institution_matches.title: SymAnt: Grounding Long-Horizon Action Anticipation with Adaptable Symbolic Priors
institution_matches.overview: The paper presents SymAnt, a neuro-symbolic framework for long-horizon action anticipation that constructs a symbolic context by jointly searching over scene graphs and knowledge graphs from a short input video, enabling unified reasoning over spatial relations, object attributes, affordances, and associated actions. SymAnt uses this symbolic context as a prior for an iterative refinement process that progressively generates and improves future action sequences, allowing parameter-efficient anticipation from short observation windows and enabling users to directly edit the underlying knowledge to adjust predictions without retraining. Experiments on five diverse datasets—Breakfast, 50 Salads, EPIC-KITCHENS, EGTEA Gaze+, and Assembly101—show that SymAnt is effective for long-horizon action anticipation, particularly when only short observation contexts are available.

institution_matches.title: Same Label, Different Interface: Beyond Action-Space Labels in Robot Learning
institution_matches.institution: New York University; UC San Diego
institution_matches.overview: The paper empirically studies how differences in the full executed action interface—encompassing filtering, physical scaling, reference construction, feedback, timing, and effort limits—affect robot learning outcomes, arguing that comparing “position” versus “velocity” actions by label alone is misleading. Across three contact-rich Factory tasks (PegInsert, GearMesh, NutThread), varying only the physical action scale within the same position-feedback law changes sample-median evaluation success by 0.645–1.000, and altering exponential moving average filtering produces task-dependent performance changes, indicating strong sensitivity to interface details. Even when the authors cross-calibrate a velocity interface to match a position interface’s local raw-torque command gain, residual sample-median performance gaps remain on PegInsert and GearMesh (with NutThread’s interval including zero), showing that equalizing a single gain does not establish trained-outcome equivalence, and motivating that action-interface studies should fully report the executed pathway and the matched physical quantities.

institution_matches.title: Securing the Robotics Supply Chain
institution_matches.overview: The paper argues that securing the robotics supply chain requires a decade-scale, sustained federal research and investment agenda distinct from general AI funding, recognizing robotics as its own supply chain with specific points of failure. It identifies major current gaps in methods for verifying and certifying components of uncertain origin, in foundational hardware research that has been underfunded relative to software, in large-scale physical test infrastructure, and in workforce development to build and maintain secure robotic systems.

topic_matches.title: TACOS: Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision for Visual Footstep Planning
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision (TACOS), which defines a continuous footstep instability score from the residual of a factor graph in legged state estimation and projects this score into preceding images to provide dense self-supervision for visual prediction of foothold stability; it introduces both a hindsight-based hard score and an immediately available causal soft score. On 1,716 manually annotated foot contacts, both TACOS variants outperform state-of-the-art alternative metrics in detecting instability and ranking its severity, improving pooled severity ranking performance by 28% over the strongest baseline. In three outdoor test runs, TACOS-based supervision yields the most accurate visual predictor of terrain stability, improving rank correlation by 58% over the strongest alternative and by an additional 25% when augmented with onboard context, and in a 50 m forest trial the trained predictor handles non-geometric terrain (mud, vegetation) while stepping around geometric obstacles (fallen branches).

topic_matches.title: FORGE: Feasible Online Reduced-Order Reference Generation and Whole-Body Execution for Agile Humanoid Locomotion
topic_matches.institution: California Institute of Technology; The University of Texas at El Paso
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents FORGE, a two-stage learning framework for agile humanoid locomotion that first trains a command-conditioned whole-body reference generator in a reduced-order single-rigid-body space with full humanoid kinematics, then uses the frozen reduced-order policy online to generate references for training a whole-body tracking policy on the full-order dynamics model. By learning a kino-dynamically consistent reference generator in the simplified space, FORGE can produce locomotion references over a broad command space and multiple strategies within a single unified framework, which are then tracked by a single whole-body policy. On the Unitree G1 humanoid, the learned policies achieve longitudinal velocities from −2.0 m/s to 2.8 m/s, lateral velocities up to ±1.0 m/s, angular velocities up to ±3.0 rad/s, one-legged hopping, and continuous transitions across commands using one unified reference policy and one whole-body tracking policy.

topic_matches.title: METATRON: A Promptable Whole-Body Execution Layer for Humanoids
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces Metatron, a promptable whole-body execution layer for humanoids that combines a generative base policy—trained on motion capture, synthetic recovery, and retargeted scene-interaction data—with a programmable skill layer that issues partial goal prompts such as timed body-part targets, velocity commands, and style cues. In Metatron, stateful code-level skills transform task intent into prompts at each control step, and the frozen base policy converts these into coordinated full-body motions; coding agents can analyze motion data and synthesize compact skill programs without task-specific retraining of the policy. On the physical Unitree G1, a single frozen Metatron checkpoint supports walking, recovery, teleoperated object pickup, and sitting on furniture with higher reaching success and push robustness than reference-tracking baselines, and the same recipe extends to climbing and acrobatics in simulation, demonstrating that new skills can be realized purely by code over a fixed motor policy.

topic_matches.title: SKiD-SLAM: Resource-Aware Distributed Multi-Robot LiDAR SLAM for Planetary Missions with Field Deployments at Analog Sites
topic_matches.institution: Inha University; Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents SKiD-SLAM, a distributed multi-robot LiDAR SLAM system designed for planetary exploration that selects communication- and computation-efficient modules for place recognition, relative pose estimation, and distributed trajectory fusion based on surveyed resource budgets of actual missions. SKiD-SLAM is validated in simulation and on public planetary-like datasets, and in two real-world field deployments (lava-tube cave exploration with wheeled rovers and crater-and-rock surface exploration with quadrupeds in South Korea), where it reliably performs distributed multi-robot LiDAR SLAM under a 250 kbps inter-robot communication budget.

topic_matches.title: MATCH: Execution-Aware Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environment
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes MATCH, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for VLN-CE that jointly learns a language-conditioned planner and a goal-conditioned primitive-action executor using an execution-aware topological graph, executor value estimates, realized outcome memory, and bounded continuous target offsets. MATCH introduces a transition-aware dense macro reward and a staged curriculum with synchronized on-policy updates, enabling the planner and executor to co-adapt such that executor-learned behaviors inform planner requests. On the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks, MATCH with 0.5B parameters achieves state-of-the-art performance among reported methods, and preliminary real-robot deployments show that the learned policies are practically executable on physical robots.

topic_matches.title: What Should a Navigator Remember? Spatiotemporal Memory for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Navigation
topic_matches.institution: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; Tsinghua University
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes a zero-shot VLN system that organizes information into complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories—combining instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation histories anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry—processed by an 8B observer and an 8B reasoner that select waypoint intents or request additional views for a geometric controller to execute. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the full spatiotemporal memory system achieves the highest performance among evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines; ablating temporal memory sharply increases average path length from 16.9 m to 39.1 m and reduces success rate, while removing the spatial map and planning component also degrades success rate. In real-world tests on a Unitree Go2 robot in corridor and office environments, the proposed zero-shot method attains higher success rates than a post-trained baseline, and LAW2 instruction-intervention evaluations indicate that preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory improves instruction following beyond endpoint success.

topic_matches.title: Proprioceptive Finger Force Estimation for Reliable Box Manipulation
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces FEEL (Finger External-Force Estimation from Proprioceptive SignaLs), an uncertainty-aware residual method that combines a calibrated virtual-spring model with a Mixture Density Network–predicted residual distribution to estimate per-finger external force magnitudes from proprioceptive histories without dedicated contact sensors. Across ten fingers and contact forces from 0–20 N, FEEL achieves a mean RMSE of 0.251 N, reducing force-estimation error by 92.8% relative to the virtual-spring baseline and by 9.4% relative to an end-to-end MDN approach. In a box pick-and-place task, using FEEL-based per-finger force adaptation maintains 10/10 task successes and raises both damage-free outcomes and overall reliability from 7/10 to 10/10 compared to open-loop finger commands.

topic_matches.title: ELEVATE: Agentic Controller Acquisition from Task Failure for Quadrupedal Manipulation
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents ELEVATE, a framework in which persistent task-program failures for a quadrupedal manipulator trigger a coding agent to autonomously formulate and refine reinforcement-learning problems (rewards, curricula, termination) to acquire missing whole-body control capabilities and add them to a reusable controller library. Starting from a single pretrained loco-manipulation controller, ELEVATE learns additional controllers for wall-supported elevation, supported manipulation, and wall descent over seven simulated tasks, and reuses these capabilities to achieve mean success rates of 98.4%–100% on the five tasks that lie beyond the initial controller’s workspace across five independent runs, whereas coding-agent baselines with a fixed controller set fail on these tasks. The task programs and controllers learned in simulation transfer to a physical quadrupedal manipulator without real-robot training or fine-tuning, achieving 18/20 successes in rack retrieval and 16/20 in floor-to-rack placement.

topic_matches.title: Skeleton-Guided Geometry-Aware Auto-Labeling for Robotic Grasping: From 4-DoF Learning to 6-DoF Execution
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes a straight-skeleton-based auto-labeling pipeline that generates two-finger grasp keypoints and feasible grasp regions, along with SkelGG-CNN, a 4-DoF grasp prediction architecture that learns geometric grasp features from skeleton-based guidance, and a generalized quasi-3D skeletonization method that extends auto-labeling to 6-DoF grasping directly on point clouds. Trained on automatically generated 4-DoF labels, SkelGG-CNN attains grasp prediction accuracies of 95.42%, 96.55%, and 97.1% on Jacquard V1, Jacquard V2, and Cornell datasets, respectively; the 6-DoF auto-labeling pipeline reaches an average precision of 18.33 on the GraspNet novel split, comparable to state-of-the-art model-based methods. In simulation, the 6-DoF method achieves grasp success rates of 98.4% on Dex-Net and 89.1% on EGAD!, and real-world tests with a Delta parallel robot report success rates of 97.4% on single household objects and 95.0% in cluttered scenes, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches without domain adaptation while providing scalable, geometry-aware annotations.

topic_matches.title: A Multi-Layer Navigation System for Smart Wheelchairs with a Limited Input Interface
topic_matches.institution: Ca’ Foscari University of Venice; European Centre for Living Technology; Padua Neuroscience Center, University of Padova; University of Padova
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents a Multi-Layer Navigation System (MLNS) for smart wheelchairs that integrates a Virtual Sensors-Driven Potential Fields method accounting for the wheelchair’s true size for obstacle detection, a Model Predictive Control module for trajectory generation, an open-vocabulary vision module for target identification, and a Priority Queue–based mechanism for target selection. The proposed MLNS is designed to interpret and safely contextualize users’ high-level intentions, including when commands are limited or faulty, enabling navigation in unknown environments while mitigating risks from misinterpreted inputs or environmental perceptions. Experiments on a physical smart wheelchair with 10 able-bodied participants, including scenarios with faulty input interfaces, show that the system operates robustly and effectively in real-world environments, indicating its potential suitability for assistive applications.
